Designing `createRegistry()` in `src/registry.ts` to return isolated state. The `registerDefaultRules` helper will accept an optional registry parameter. It will fall back to the module-level default register when omitted. Tests must pass regardless of execution order after pipeline side-effects. The CLI must continue registering defaults exactly once.

The CLI currently registers defaults through a side-effect import of `register-default-rules`. The `registerDefaultRules` helper will accept a `RuleRegistry` parameter. The CLI side-effect import will call it directly, preserving default registration without duplication. Tests will instantiate fresh registries via `createRegistry()` and pass them to the helper.

`src/registry.ts` will define a `RuleRegistry` interface with `register`, `getEnabled`, and `list` methods. `createRegistry()` will return a fresh instance backed by an isolated array.

`createRegistry()` will expose `getEnabled` and `list` methods alongside `register`. The module-level default registry will be created by calling `createRegistry()` once. Existing `register` and related exports will be preserved as wrappers around that default instance. `analyzeFiles` will accept an optional `RuleRegistry` parameter so callers can supply their own isolated registry.

I am reconsidering the function signatures. Passing `registry` as a fifth positional parameter after `resolvedFiles` feels awkward. I am exploring whether to place it inside `pipelineOptions` or use an options object instead, following the pattern used by `runPipeline`.

Positional registry parameters are acceptable per the bead requirements. `fixFiles` will propagate the optional registry through to `runPipeline`. `registry.test.ts` will instantiate fresh registries via `createRegistry()` inside each test or describe block to guarantee order independence and survive vic-pipeline side-effects. `vic-pipeline.test.ts` may need minimal updates.

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
The rule pipeline preserves original tabs without calling fix, likely because no violations trigger fixes. This differs from the legacy path.

Legacy always re-prints function declarations via the printer, even when the order is unchanged. The rule path only applies fixes when violations exist, so it leaves content untouched when no issues are found.

AC3 requires rule-based output to be canonical. Legacy must be aligned to match rule behavior rather than leaving differences as documented divergences. For circular dependencies, legacy reorders and reprints even though circular dependencies are not fixable by the rule path.

Rule analysis filters out circular violations, so the rule path returns the original file unchanged. Legacy still reorders declarations via topological sort, which may alter cycle order or formatting. To align legacy with rule behavior, it should return the input byte-identical when no actionable violations exist.

The legacy path should mirror the rule pipeline by skipping rewrites entirely when no actionable violations exist. Currently `fixParsedFile` compares `fixedContent` against the original `content`, but this comparison does not prevent unnecessary reordering. The fix is to return the original file unchanged whenever the analysis finds no stepdown or nested violations.

The printer always reformats whitespace, turning tabs into spaces even on no-op files. The rule path avoids this by skipping the printer entirely when no violations exist. The fix is to guard `fixParsedFile` with a check for actionable violations—stepdown or nested function violations—before reordering. If none exist, the original content is returned unchanged.

The proposed guard in `fixParsedFile` returns the original content unchanged when no actionable violations exist. This handles circular dependencies and `test-correct` correctly, since both lack stepdown or nested violations. The remaining concern is whether callers ever pass an undefined `analysisResult`, which would bypass the guard.

Fixing `fixParsedFile` is within v3a scope. The affected files are `src/fixer.ts` and `src/analyzer.ts`. When violations exist, both pipelines print identical output because they share the same printer. The guard should only skip reordering when no actionable violations exist.

I will check analyzer-fixer-unified and other tests that expect legacy reformatting. The short-circuit fix will be implemented and followed by re-running characterization tests. When analysisResult is omitted, fixParsedFile builds its own dependency graph and always reprints, which is acceptable for those paths.

The `fixParsedFile` guard now returns the original content unchanged whenever `analysisResult` contains no stepdown or nested violations. This aligns the legacy path with the rule pipeline for files that have no actionable issues. Next, re-run the characterization tests and the full fixer suite.
</details></think>
